extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal practitioners, and scholars studying English common law
extracted.subtask_description: Foundational principles and rules governing English law: nature and reception of customs, civil and canon law, categories of statutes, and established rules of statutory construction (Blackstone's Commentaries excerpt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty requirement (id certum est)
rubrics_metrics.description: A thing may be uncertain in value yet good if the value may at any time be ascertained: 'id certum est, quod certum reddi potest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a yearly holding's value may be uncertain but acceptable because it can be ascertained later. (Footnote: 1 Roll. Abr. 565.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Customs must be compulsory
rubrics_metrics.description: Customs, though established by consent, must be (when established) compulsory, and not left to the option of every man whether he will use them or no.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A custom that all inhabitants shall be rated toward maintenance of a bridge is good; a custom that every man contributes at his own pleasure is idle and no custom at all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customs must be consistent with each other
rubrics_metrics.description: Customs must be consistent; one custom cannot be set up in opposition to another because contradictory customs cannot both be good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: If custom gives a right to windows into another's garden, another custom cannot validly allow obstructing those windows; one should deny existence of the contradictory custom. (Footnote: 9 Rep. 58.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Special/customary laws in derogation of common law construed strictly
rubrics_metrics.description: Customs that derogate from the common law must be construed strictly and pursued exactly as established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Under gavelkind, an infant of fifteen may convey lands by a particular species of conveyance (feoffment) but that custom does not empower other conveyances or leasing for seven years. (Co. Cop. Sec. 33.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Customs and king's prerogative (special customs subordinate)
rubrics_metrics.description: All special customs must submit to the king's prerogative; customary rules may yield to sovereign prerogatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Lands of the nature of gavelkind purchased by the king nonetheless descend to the king's eldest son on the king's demise. (Co. Litt. 15 b.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil and canon law reception depends on custom or parliamentary adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil and canon laws are received in England only because they have been admitted by immemorial usage/custom in particular cases or introduced by consent of parliament; their authority is not intrinsic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone follows Hale: their force here arises from local reception or parliamentary adoption (see statute 25 Hen. VIII. c. 21 quoted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil and canon laws are subordinate and have limited jurisdictions
rubrics_metrics.description: The civil (Roman) and canon laws, where received, are subordinate branches ('leges sub graviori lege') and apply only in certain courts and jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts where they may be used include: (1) ecclesiastical courts (archbishops/bishops), (2) military courts, (3) admiralty courts, and (4) the courts of the two universities. Their reception is grounded on custom and sometimes statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common law superintends and controls civil/canon courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Common law courts have superintendency over civil and canon courts: to keep them within jurisdiction, determine excesses, restrain or prohibit such excess, and punish officers enforcing illegal sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three marks of superiority: (1) superintendency over those courts; (2) exposition of acts of parliament concerning their extent; (3) appeal to the king in last resort—showing civil/canon laws are subordinate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of statutes: general/public vs special/private
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes are either general/public (rule for the whole community, courts take notice ex officio) or special/private (operate upon particular persons/concerns and must be shown and pleaded).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 13 Eliz. c. 10 (leasing by spiritual persons) is public; an act enabling a bishop to make a sixty-year lease for A.B. is private.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of statutes: declaratory vs remedial (enlarging/restraining)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes may be declaratory of the common law (declaring what law is) or remedial (supplying defects), and remedial statutes subdivide into enlarging and restraining statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (declaratory): 25 Edw. III treason statute enumerates existing treasons; (enlarging) 5 Eliz. made clipping coin high treason; (restraining) 13 Eliz. restricted spiritual corporations' leases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction rule 1: Consider old law, mischief, and remedy (mischief rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: In construing remedial statutes judges should consider three points: the old law, the mischief the old law did not provide for, and the remedy the parliament provided; construe to suppress the mischief and advance the remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 13 Eliz. restricting long leases—leases valid during grantor's life are not within the mischief and thus not within the remedy. (3 Rep. 7 b.; Co. Litt. 11 b. 42.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction rule 2: Statutes referring to inferior rank not extended to superior
rubrics_metrics.description: A statute that treats of persons or things of an inferior rank cannot by general words be extended to those of a superior rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A statute mentioning 'deans, prebendaries, parsons, vicars, and others having spiritual promotion' does not extend to bishops though bishops have spiritual promotion. (2 Rep. 46.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction rule 3: Penal statutes construed strictly
rubrics_metrics.description: Penal statutes must be strictly construed and not extended beyond their precise terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 1 Edw. VI about stealing 'horses' was not taken to include stealing 'but one horse' without new act; 14 Geo. II c.6 'sheep or other cattle' was confined to sheep, prompting later detailed statute. (Bac. Elem. c. 12.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction rule 4: Statutes against frauds construed liberally
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes against frauds are to be liberally and beneficially expounded when they act upon the offence (voiding fraudulent transactions), though penal consequences are to be construed strictly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 13 Eliz. c. 5 voiding gifts made to defraud creditors was held to extend by general words to a gift made to defraud the queen of a forfeiture. (3 Rep. 82.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction rule 5: One part construed by another to preserve whole (ut res magis valeat quam pereat)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts of a statute should be construed in light of other parts so that if possible the whole statute stands and every clause has effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: If land vested in king saving A's right and A holds a lease for three years, A shall hold for his term and then land goes to king—each clause operates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction rule 6: Savings repugnant to body of act are void
rubrics_metrics.description: A saving clause totally repugnant to the body of the act is void; otherwise it would render the statute ineffective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Vesting land in king saving the right of all persons whatsoever would be repugnant and void, so land vests absolutely. (1 Rep. 47.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction rule 7: Statute overrules common law; later statutes may repeal earlier ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Where common law and statute differ, the common law gives place to the statute; an old statute gives place to a new one when the latter is couched in negative terms or necessarily implies a negative; but two affirmative acts that can stand together have concurrent efficacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: If earlier act requires £20 and later act says twenty marks, latter implies negative and repeals former. Concurrent jurisdiction example: an offence made indictable at different courts may be prosecuted at either unless later statute expressly confines jurisdiction. (Jenk. Cent. 2. 73.; 11 Rep. 63.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction rule 8: Repeal of repealing act revives the original statute
rubrics_metrics.description: If a statute repeals another and that repealing statute is itself later repealed, the first statute is revived without formal words of revival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Statutes of 26 and 35 Hen. VIII declaring supremacy were impliedly revived after intermediate repeals. (4 Inst. 325.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction rule 9: Acts derogatory from subsequent parliaments' power do not bind
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts of parliament which purport to restrict the power of subsequent parliaments are not binding on later parliaments; the legislature cannot bind its successors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 11 Hen. VII c.1 (protection for assisting king de facto) is good only as to common prosecutions and will not restrain parliamentary attainder. (4 Inst. 43.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction rule 10: Statutes impossible to perform or producing absurd collateral consequences void quoad hoc
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts of parliament impossible to perform are of no validity, and collateral absurd consequences contradictory to common reason may be disregarded by judges quoad hoc; but judges should not reject a main statute merely because it is unreasonable when words are clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: An act giving a man power to try all causes in his manor is construed not to extend to causes where he is a party; but if parliament positively enacts he may try his own causes with express words, courts cannot defeat that legislative intent. (8 Rep. 118.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of equity courts (limits and purposes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts of equity exist to assist, moderate, and explain the common law: to correct rigour, detect latent frauds, enforce trusts binding in conscience though not strictly legal, and relieve bona fide objects of relief; typically concerned with matters of property and cannot override criminal law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity relieves cases where letter of law induces apparent hardship, but criminal cases must conform to letter of law; equity may result in less punishment but not more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory effect by citation and form (how statutes are cited)
rubrics_metrics.description: Antient statutes are cited by place or subject or initial words; more usual modern method is by regnal year and chapter number (e.g., 9 Geo. II. c. 4), since acts of one session form one statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance on citation conventions for statutes (useful for legal drafting and reference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and composition of Roman civil law and corpus juris civilis
rubrics_metrics.description: Roman law (civil law) historically consists of: (1) the Institutes, (2) the Digests/Pandects, (3) the Code (new code of imperial constitutions), and (4) the Novels; together forming the corpus juris civilis as published under Justinian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note relevant when citing or using Roman law materials to illustrate or inform English law reasoning; notes on rediscovery and influence in Europe.
